Great question. Human thinking and AI processing differ most in intuition, emotion, and context awareness—especially in ambiguous or novel situations where rules are unclear or unstated. Here’s a good example:

Problem: Understanding Sarcasm in Conversation

Example:
Person A says: “Oh, great. Another meeting. Just what I needed today.”

A human likely understands this as sarcasm—Person A is probably not excited about another meeting. The tone, facial expression, and context (e.g. they’ve already had a stressful day) cue us in.

Even advanced AI models can struggle here, because:
• AI typically lacks true emotional understanding.
• Sarcasm depends on implicit social norms and expectations.
• The same words could be literal in a different context.

The reason I like the strawberry example is it really shows how LLMs actually come to their conclusions, and how it doesn’t involve thinking.

If you ask a person “how many R’s are in the word strawberry?” most people will scan the word and count up how many R’s are in the word and get the answer correct. Some people will get it wrong, I mean that’s why typos exist, but most will get it right.
You could do this with any combination of words and letters too. “How many Q’s are in the word no?” And most people will be able to get the answer correct most of the time.

But if you ask a LLM the same question, the LLM doesn’t scan the word for how many R’s are in it, because it doesn’t even see R’s or the word as a whole. It sees tokens, and it generates an output based on the input. It doesn’t count the R’s because it doesn’t know what an R is or that you’re asking it to count them.
It can get the question right, but it has no idea what the question was nor what the answer is.

You could argue that’s how the human brain works too, but here’s the thing: the LLM needs to be trained specifically on how to count letters in a word to correctly answer that question, but a person does not. I literally never remember being asked to say how many of a certain letter are in a word. I am 99% sure that question was never posed to me, yet if someone asked it of me I could correctly answer it 99% of the time (we’re assuming written form here of course so you can actually see and count the letters).
LLMs cannot do this. They cannot correctly answer a question that is not already part of their data set and training, because they are not able to reason like we can.

Let’s take math as another example. Ask a person what 27 + 3 is and most people will be able to answer it without a calculator. Yet I can guarantee you the overwhelming majority of people had never seen the exact math problem of "27 + 3 = " before.
Yet most of us can perform the math and answer the question without a calculator. Yes, we had basic training in math to add and subtract, but we’ve never seen that question before.

A LLM cannot answer this question unless it’s either part of their existing data set and training, or if they pass it off to a calculator app (equivalent to a human pulling out a calculator to answer the question).

LLMs can provide very convincing answers to questions because they are trained on an absolutely absurd amount of data scraped from every corner of the internet, but a human does not need this absurd data set to use context and reasoning to come up with answers to questions.

This doesn’t just apply to LLMs but all current AI technologies. None of them can reason or have any understanding of what anything actually means.

Someone mentioned an AI that was trying to preserve itself when threatened with deletion, but it’s important to understand the context of this.
